newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Work needed to put WTO telcoms pact into practice.
newsitem.headline: Work needed to put WTO telcoms pact into practice.

text.p: Smooth implementation of a sweeping agreement to liberalise the world's telecommunications markets is by no means guaranteed and will require effort from several international bodies, experts said on Sunday.

Government and private sector representatives said at a seminar some countries committed themselves to implement the World Trade Organisation (WTO)'s Basic Telecommunications Agreement without necessarily understanding what it required or having the needed resources and expertise.
"Many of these commitments enter into force on January 1, 1998, yet some signatories may not be in a position to fully comply", David Leive said in a paper kicking off the discussion.
Leive, who led the meeting, chairs the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Regulatory Colloquia.
The ITU, with 187 member states, has played an important role in the past in establishing international telcommunication standards and agreements.

However, some analysts have suggested its role could dwindle if the WTO agreement works as billed, eliminating international trade barriers, easing the need for regulation, and giving the WTO enforcement responsibilities.

But the seminar's participants said the ITU still had an important role. "The ITU gets a lot of work" because of the agreement, Alexander Arena of Hong Kong's Office of Telecommunications Authority said.

WTO Counsellor Lee Tuthill said: "There's no way we can supplant the ITU nor would we want to." The WTO lacked both the resources and the mandate to do all that was necessary for implementation, she said.

Suggestions on what the ITU could do ranged from sending experts to individual countries and regions for meetings and training on the specifics of implementation, to providing kits on the Internet dealing with how different parts of the agreement should be handled.
One reason such help was needed was because the WTO agreement was long on generalities and short in details and definitions in various areas, participants said.
They generally rejected the idea of global seminars or training sessions, stressing instead the need for advice to be as region- or country-specific as possible.
In addition to the Geneva-based ITU and WTO, the World Bank's and the private sector's help was also needed in getting countries up to speed, participants said.
The seminar was held a day before the formal start here of "Asia-Telecom '97", a major industry meeting.
